svg.title: NF2-related schwannomatosis: how one gene explains both multiple meningiomas and bilateral vestibular schwannomas
svg.desc: Schematic of how NF2-related schwannomatosis explains both multiple meningiomas and bilateral vestibular schwannomas through a single gene. It opens with the naming panel, headed "this is not a rename, the term was retired", quoting the 2022 international consensus word for word: "In the revised nomenclature, the term neurofibromatosis 2 has been retired to improve diagnostic specificity." The new name is NF2-related schwannomatosis, abbreviated NF2-SWN; the reasoning is to emphasise the overlap in how these conditions present and to reduce misdiagnosis as neurofibromatosis type 1; the new criteria also write the mosaic form directly into the text; and searching with an old report that says "NF2" turns up two sets of vocabulary that refer to the same thing without being identical. At the centre of the figure sits one node: NF2, on chromosome 22. Three things are written on it: NF2-SWN is an autosomal dominant tumour predisposition syndrome whose carriers are prone to schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas; NF2 is also the commonest driver mutation in sporadic meningioma, which is why Alliance A071401 enrolled only meningiomas with a somatic NF2 mutation, its stated design reason being "the predominance of NF2 mutations in meningiomas"; and someone growing both tumours is showing two exits from the same broken road. Two branches run from that node. The left branch is multiple meningiomas: up to 80% of people with NF2-SWN develop a meningioma over a lifetime, from a meta-analysis of 15 studies, 937 patients and 3,637 tumours; the 2,082 tumours under surveillance grew at a weighted mean of 0.508 cubic centimetres a year; new meningiomas appeared during surveillance in 24.6% of patients, though the 95% confidence interval is very wide at 2.73 to 58.7 and only three studies had data; only 203 tumours were surgically removed, with a pooled recurrence risk of 12.5%, and 665 had stereotactic radiosurgery, with a progression risk of 6.29%; and the international consensus adds that about 10% grow quickly, one study defining quickly as more than 2 cubic centimetres a year, and that 20% of patients grow a new meningioma. The right branch is bilateral vestibular schwannomas: on their own sufficient for the diagnosis of NF2-SWN; imaging intervals have to be adjusted because growth rates vary more in this group than in sporadic tumours and imaging may need to be more frequent; and in someone with bilateral tumours the growth rate on one side may accelerate after the tumour on the other side is removed. Below the branches a note warns to watch the denominators, since surgery and radiosurgery together account for far fewer tumours than surveillance, so "up to 80% will grow one" is not "80% of people need treatment". A further passage connects to the radiation side: in radiation-induced meningiomas, point mutations in NF2 are less common than in sporadic ones while gene fusion events are more common, thought to follow faulty repair of radiation-induced double-strand breaks - the same gene broken by two entirely different mechanisms. The criteria follow, any one of which is enough for the diagnosis: first, bilateral vestibular schwannomas; second, the same pathogenic NF2 variant found in at least two anatomically distinct NF2-related tumours, that is schwannoma, meningioma or ependymoma, with the note that if the variant allele frequency in unaffected tissue such as blood is clearly below 50% the diagnosis is the mosaic form; and third, two major criteria or one major plus two minor criteria, where the major criteria are a unilateral vestibular schwannoma, a first-degree relative other than a sibling with NF2-SWN, two or more meningiomas with a single one counting only as a minor criterion, and a pathogenic NF2 variant in unaffected tissue, while the minor criteria are ependymoma, meningioma, schwannoma, juvenile cataract, retinal hamartoma and epiretinal membrane under the age of 40. Two easily mistaken points are listed alongside: there is no upper age limit on bilateral vestibular schwannomas, a cut-off at 70 having been proposed in 2019 and rejected by the consensus in order to "avoid clinicians not investigating older patients"; and for a unilateral vestibular schwannoma with two or more schwannomas at other sites, an LZTR1 variant should be excluded before NF2-SWN is confirmed. Next comes the hearing response to bevacizumab, preceded by its response definition: in all three prospective trials the primary endpoint was a hearing response defined on word recognition score, an improvement in the proportion of a standard word list understood and maintained for a period of time, and not a subjective sense of hearing better. Three figures follow, each with its population: in 14 patients with NF2 and progressive hearing loss in the target ear treated for 46 weeks, the confirmed hearing response was 5 of 14, or 36%, with a 95% confidence interval of 13 to 65%, the response defined as improvement maintained for three months or more, and no patient having worse hearing; in a high-dose trial of 22 patients at six months it was 9 of 22, or 41%, with the authors concluding that the high dose does not appear more effective than the standard dose; and in a systematic review of 9 studies and 176 patients, hearing improved in 36%, was stable in 46% and worse in 18%, while tumours partially shrank in 40%, were stable in 50% and progressed in 10%, with serious adverse events in 13% and the authors noting that some tumours regrew after treatment stopped. A maintenance trial of 20 patients shows the time dimension, with target ears free of hearing deterioration in 95% at 48 weeks, 89% at 72 weeks and 70% at 98 weeks. The panel notes that this road is open only for NF2-related vestibular schwannomas, the 2020 European guideline putting it briefly that except for bevacizumab in NF2 there is no role for pharmacotherapy, and that people with a sporadic tumour should not apply these figures to themselves. A full band across the foot of the figure carries the differential: multiple meningiomas do not equal NF2. It lists SMARCB1, that is SMARCB1-related schwannomatosis, also on chromosome 22, which can likewise give multiple intracranial meningiomas; LZTR1, the one to exclude when a unilateral vestibular schwannoma comes with schwannomas elsewhere; BAP1 tumour predisposition syndrome where there are no schwannomas; SUFU-related familial meningioma predisposition; SMARCE1, which causes familial clear cell meningioma; and past radiation exposure, the line most often skipped, because meningioma is a common second tumour long after radiation and 17.3% of radiation-induced meningiomas are multiple. The same panel quotes the international consensus: compared with sporadic cases, people with NF2-SWN present younger and are more likely to grow multiple meningiomas, so anyone presenting like this should be screened for germline NF2 and SMARCE1 variants, with whether and how that is done belonging to a genetic counselling clinic rather than to booking a test yourself. The mosaic panel follows: among 1,055 de novo cases with no family history in the previous generation, 232, or 22.0%, were confirmed or presumed mosaic; because the detection rate for non-mosaic variants is itself only 36.7%, the authors estimate the overall mosaic proportion may be as high as 59.7%; the proportion varies sharply with age at presentation, 21.7% among those presenting with bilateral vestibular schwannomas under 20 and 80.7% among those aged 60 and over; someone with the mosaic form can still be severely affected and needs full clinical surveillance and intervention; and testing is not one tube of blood, since blood is tested and ideally two or more related tumours from different regions of the nervous system as well, to tell the mosaic form from a germline variant. A red band across that panel states plainly that the figure gives no percentage for a relative's risk, because that has to be worked out by a genetic counsellor from the patient's own test results. The Taiwanese section closes the figure in two cells. Found: the reimbursement text does carry the role of a genetic counselling centre, the rules for 25021B, chromosome study (special), stating word for word that it is restricted to genetic counselling centres accredited by the Ministry of Health and Welfare and that use as a general screening test is outside reimbursement. Not found: there is no test item anywhere in the schedule named for NF2 or neurofibromatosis, and whether NF2-SWN appears on the published Taiwanese rare disease list cannot be retrieved, since Article 3 of the Rare Disease Control and Orphan Drug Act says the central competent authority designates and publishes it on a prevalence basis - the legal basis is findable but the list is not, so a genetic counselling centre has to be asked. The figure ends by advising that the family history be written out as a table before the appointment - who has had a brain or spinal tumour, hearing problems, a juvenile cataract, because several of the criteria depend on it - and that the question in the room is whether this presentation needs a genetic counselling referral, rather than booking a test first.

g.text: NF2-RELATED SCHWANNOMATOSIS
One gene, two tumours:
multiple meningiomas and
bilateral vestibular
schwannomas
If the report says two or more meningiomas, or a
vestibular schwannoma in each ear, this figure is drawn
for you.
This is not a question to split between two clinics and ask
half of in each; every figure here carries its tumour type
and its cohort, and because the designs and endpoints
differ, the data points must not be compared directly.
This is not a rename; the term was retired
"In the revised nomenclature, the term
neurofibromatosis 2 has been retired to improve
diagnostic specificity."
A 2022 international consensus reorganised the names and
diagnostic criteria for this family of conditions. The new name is
NF2-related schwannomatosis, abbreviated NF2-SWN; the
reasoning is to emphasise the overlap in how these conditions
present and to reduce misdiagnosis as neurofibromatosis type
1. The new criteria also write the mosaic form directly into the
text. If you search with an old report that says "NF2", you will
find two sets of vocabulary; they refer to the same thing, but the
new criteria are not identical to the old ones.
NF2 (chromosome 22)
NF2-SWN is an autosomal dominant tumour
predisposition syndrome, and carriers are prone to
schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas
NF2 is also the commonest driver mutation in sporadic
meningioma - Alliance A071401 enrolled only
meningiomas with a somatic NF2 mutation, and its stated
design reason is "the predominance of NF2 mutations in
meningiomas"
Someone growing both tumours is showing two exits
from the same broken road
Multiple meningiomas
Up to 80% of people with NF2-SWN develop a meningioma over
a lifetime (a meta-analysis of 15 studies, 937 patients and
3,637 tumours)
The 2,082 tumours under surveillance grew at a weighted
mean of 0.508 cm3 a year
New meningiomas appeared during surveillance in 24.6% of
patients, but the 95% confidence interval is very wide (2.73 to
58.7) and only three studies had data
Only 203 tumours were surgically removed (pooled
recurrence risk 12.5%), and 665 had stereotactic
radiosurgery (progression risk 6.29%)
The international consensus adds that about 10% grow quickly
(one study defined quickly as more than 2 cm3 a year) and that
20% of patients grow a new meningioma
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are on their own sufficient
for the diagnosis of NF2-SWN
How often imaging is done has to be adjusted: growth rates
vary more in this group than in sporadic tumours, and
imaging may need to be more frequent
In someone with bilateral tumours, the growth rate on one
side may accelerate after the tumour on the other side is
removed
Watch the denominators: surgery and radiosurgery
together account for far fewer tumours than surveillance
does - "up to 80% will grow one" is not "80% of people need
treatment".
One more layer connects to the radiation side: in
radiation-induced meningiomas, point mutations in NF2 are
less common than in sporadic ones, while gene fusion events
are more common, thought to follow faulty repair of
radiation-induced double-strand breaks. The same gene,
broken by two entirely different mechanisms.
What the criteria say: any one of these is enough
for the diagnosis
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas
The same pathogenic NF2 variant found in at least
two anatomically distinct NF2-related tumours
(schwannoma, meningioma or ependymoma)
Note: if the variant allele frequency in unaffected tissue
such as blood is clearly below 50%, the diagnosis is the
mosaic form
Two major criteria, or one major criterion plus two
minor criteria
Major criteria: a unilateral vestibular schwannoma; a
first-degree relative other than a sibling with NF2-SWN;
two or more meningiomas (a single one counts only as a
minor criterion); a pathogenic NF2 variant found in
unaffected tissue
Minor criteria: ependymoma, meningioma, schwannoma,
plus juvenile cataract, retinal hamartoma and epiretinal
membrane under the age of 40
There is no upper age limit on bilateral vestibular
schwannomas
A cut-off at 70 was proposed in 2019; the consensus decided
against it, in its own words to "avoid clinicians not investigating
older patients"
With a unilateral tumour plus schwannomas elsewhere,
exclude LZTR1 first
For a unilateral vestibular schwannoma with two or more
schwannomas at other sites, an LZTR1 variant should be
excluded before NF2-SWN is confirmed
The "hearing response" to bevacizumab only
makes sense with its response definition
In all three prospective trials the primary endpoint was a
hearing response defined on word recognition score - an
improvement in the proportion of a standard word list
understood, maintained for a period of time. It is not a
subjective sense of hearing better.
14 patients with NF2 and progressive hearing loss in the target ear,
treated for 46 weeks
95% confidence interval 13 to 65%; the response definition is
improvement maintained for three months or more; no patient had
worse hearing
A high-dose trial of 22 patients, at six months
The authors conclude that the high dose does not appear more effective
than the standard dose
A systematic review of 9 studies and 176 patients
hearing improved in 36%
stable in 46%, worse in 18%; tumours partially shrank in 40%, were
stable in 50% and progressed in 10%; serious adverse events 13%, and
the authors note that some tumours regrew after treatment stopped
A maintenance trial of 20 patients shows the time dimension: the proportion of target ears free of hearing deterioration
48 weeks
72 weeks
98 weeks
This road is open only for NF2-related vestibular
schwannomas. The 2020 European vestibular schwannoma
guideline puts it briefly: except for bevacizumab in NF2, there
is no role for pharmacotherapy. People with a sporadic
tumour should not apply these figures to themselves.
Multiple meningiomas do not equal NF2
Two meningiomas on a report is not the same thing as NF2. This is
the differential list from the same review.
SMARCB1
SMARCB1-related schwannomatosis, also on chromosome 22,
can likewise give multiple intracranial meningiomas
LZTR1
The one to exclude when a unilateral vestibular schwannoma
comes with schwannomas elsewhere
BAP1
Where there are no schwannomas, there is also BAP1 tumour
predisposition syndrome
SUFU
SUFU-related familial meningioma predisposition
SMARCE1
SMARCE1, which causes familial clear cell meningioma
Past radiation exposure
The last line is the one most often skipped: the history has to ask
about past radiation exposure, because meningioma is a
common second tumour long after radiation - and among
radiation-induced meningiomas, 17.3% are multiple
The international consensus puts it this way: compared with
sporadic cases, people with NF2-SWN present younger and are
more likely to grow multiple meningiomas, so anyone presenting
like this should be screened for germline NF2 and SMARCE1
variants. Whether and how that is done belongs to a genetic
counselling clinic, not to booking a test yourself.
The mosaic form: the variant is present in only
some cells
Among 1,055 de novo cases with no family history in the
previous generation, 232 (22.0%) were confirmed or presumed
mosaic
Because the detection rate for non-mosaic variants is itself only
36.7%, the authors estimate the overall mosaic proportion may
be as high as 59.7%
The proportion varies sharply with age at presentation: 21.7%
among those presenting with bilateral vestibular schwannomas
under the age of 20, and 80.7% among those aged 60 and over
Someone with the mosaic form can still be severely affected
and needs full clinical surveillance and intervention
Testing is not one tube of blood: blood is tested, and ideally two
or more related tumours from different regions of the nervous
system as well, to tell the mosaic form from a germline variant
This figure gives no percentage for a relative's
risk - that has to be worked out by a genetic
counsellor from your own test results.
In Taiwan: what can be found, and what cannot
Found
The reimbursement text does carry the role of a genetic
counselling centre - the rules for 25021B, "chromosome study
(special)", state word for word that it is restricted to genetic
counselling centres accredited by the Ministry of Health and
Welfare, and that use as a general screening test is outside
reimbursement
Not found
There is no test item anywhere in the schedule named for NF2
or neurofibromatosis; and whether NF2-SWN appears on the
published Taiwanese rare disease list cannot be retrieved -
Article 3 of the Rare Disease Control and Orphan Drug Act says
the central competent authority designates and publishes it on a
prevalence basis, so the legal basis is findable but the list is not.
Ask a genetic counselling centre
Before the appointment, write the family history out as a table:
who has had a brain or spinal tumour, hearing problems, a
juvenile cataract - several of the criteria depend on it. The
question in the room is "does this presentation need a genetic
counselling referral", not booking a test first.
Schematic, redrawn from the 2022 international consensus (Plotkin 2022),
Evans 2025, the Sheppard 2026 meta-analysis, the International
Consortium on Meningiomas consensus review (Nassiri 2024), Alliance
A071401 (Brastianos 2023), Blakeley 2016, Plotkin 2019, Screnci 2024,
Plotkin 2023, Evans 2020, Krzeminska 2026, the 2020 EANO guideline and
the National Health Insurance fee schedule, rather than reproduced from
their figures; the cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies
differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
